correctness.rationale: Embedding as centered scaled coordinate simplex produces the exact directed root width maximum. Pairwise Gram classification yields exactly N=d(d+1) caps, P=d(d+1)(d-1) nearest pairs and no positive-measure triple before b=sqrt(2/3). Conditioning on the cap midpoint gives the stated exact beta lens integral. A bounded local chart and dominated convergence give B_d with nonzero sign and exponent d/2. Entire proof is analytic for every d>=3. A standalone standard-library checker verified root combinatorics in d=3..10 and the lens coefficient numerically in d=3..5; finite checks are not substituted for proof.

originality.rationale: The claim evaluates two entire adjacent upper-tail regimes of the Haar width distribution of a regular simplex, using type-A directed-edge-root caps, with an exact lens integral and nonzero first-contact coefficient. Har-Peled–Robson treats minimum width and minimizers; Finch treats first and second width moments; Kabluchko–Litvak–Zaporozhets supplies all moments, which determine the law implicitly but not an explicit cap-intersection stratification. The two closest published cap claims concern dissimilar center configurations (cube octant diagonals and regular-simplex vertices) and do not imply the directed-edge-root formula. Relevant sections of the pertinent primary full texts were inspected. The existence of a not-yet-located equivalent earlier cap calculation is a residual priority risk.
residual_risks: Moment determinacy yields a nonconstructive implicit expression for all distribution values; a historical equivalent explicit inversion may have appeared elsewhere.
A spherical root-system cap-inclusion-exclusion result not indexed in the searched literature might recover the same two transition intervals.

value.rationale: This is an all-dimensional exact two-interval law for the naturally defined random line-projection width of regular simplices. It identifies two geometrically sharp, dimension-free overlap thresholds and a nontrivial exact phase-transition coefficient, resolving distribution information not explicitly provided by known mean and higher-moment results. The special tetrahedral upper-tail uniformity is a concrete interpretable benchmark. The broader method is standard but the root-incidence and onset constants are object-specific and mathematically informative.
